doc.title: Don Wolff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: African American musicians in Hollywood and blackface in Ellington films
summary: Wolff explains how Black musicians were relegated to stereotyped roles, and recalls an early Ellington short in which a musician was darkened.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I was interested in your comment when you said in order to get Basie in Hollywood we had to see some of the kind of bad Hollywood too. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Well that’s particularly true for African American musicians who didn’t get the opportunity that white musicians got in the early part of the Hollywood history. So when we got jazz, that was one thing on film, it was another thing when we got African American jazz on film. And you see some of our great American musicians relegated to the roles that not only Hollywood placed on them, but all of America placed on them. So that was real sad to see Billie Holiday only as a maid, and Louis Armstrong only as a butler, and the only person Louis Armstrong could have a love relationship with in a movie was a horse. In those days African Americans weren’t allowed to express emotion to one another, to people.
I’ve read some really questionable things about a couple of filmings where if there was a white musician in the band they had to blacken his skin or vice versa.

The very first film of a jazz musician was a Duke Ellington film. And you are exactly correct. That’s what they did in one of the Ellington films is had to darken one of the musicians with a blackface so that he would be blacker on film than he was in real life. Even though he was an African American.
Oh, was this, I’m trying to remember, was it the saxophone player?

Yes it was the saxophone player as I recall and I think the name of the movie was, well it was one of the first Ellington short films. It was a nine minute short film, “Black and Blue” or something like that or “Bundle of Blues.”
